issues.legal_issue: A judgment-debtor is entitled to restitution of property sold to the decree-holder under a decree that was set aside when the restitution application was filed, notwithstanding that a fresh decree was later entered against the judgment-debtor.
material_facts: An ex parte decree was executed, and the decree-holder purchased the judgment-debtor’s property at the execution sale and took possession.
The decree was later set aside and the suit was remanded for rehearing.
The judgment-debtor applied for restitution after the decree was set aside but before a fresh decree was passed.
After rehearing, a fresh decree was passed against the judgment-debtor and was ultimately affirmed.
issues.conclusion: The judgment-debtor was entitled to restitution notwithstanding the later decree. The decree-holder had to restore possession, subject to the judgment-debtor depositing the amount due under the fresh decree. The judgment-debtor was not entitled to past mesne profits, but could recover future mesne profits if possession was not delivered after the required deposit.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, when a decree is varied or reversed, the court must, so far as possible, restore the parties to the positions they would have occupied but for the erroneous decree. The obligation to make restitution arises on reversal or modification and includes restoring what was done under the erroneous decree. The right is assessed by reference to the decree’s status when the restitution application was made; a later decree does not validate a sale under the set-aside decree where the decree-holder was the purchaser. The court relied on Zainal-Abdin Khan v. Muhammad Asghar Ali Khan and the principles stated in Set Umedmal v. Srinath Ray, Raghu Nandan Singh v. Jagdish Singh, Abdul Rahaman v. Sarafat Ali, and Shivbai Kom Babya Swami v. Yesoo. It distinguished Lal Bhagwant Singh v. Rai Sahib Lala Sri Kishen Das, where the decree was not reversed in a way that displaced the sale’s foundation.

rule.if: restitution_application and original_decree_set_aside and application_before_fresh_decree and decreeholder_self_purchased and later_decree_against_applicant

predicates.restitution_application: A party sought restoration of property or benefits after a decree was set aside or varied.
predicates.original_decree_set_aside: The decree under which the property was sold was set aside before the restitution application was made.
predicates.application_before_fresh_decree: The party applied for restitution before a fresh decree was passed after rehearing.
predicates.decreeholder_self_purchased: The decree-holder, rather than an independent purchaser, bought the property at the execution sale.
predicates.later_decree_against_applicant: After rehearing, a later decree was entered against the party seeking restitution.

issues.definition: When a party applies for restitution after the supporting decree has been set aside and before a fresh decree, and the decree-holder purchased the property, a later decree against the applicant does not by itself defeat restitution.
